claims.text: A combined DFT and machine-learning workflow can predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys within 5% of high-precision experimental measurements.
The targeted initial materials are single-phase HEA solid solutions at room temperature.
DFT calculations can generate the basic thermodynamic properties and phase diagrams needed by the workflow.
Machine-learning regression models trained on computed data can interpolate and predict melting-property trends across HEA composition space.
The proposed workflow is intended for ambient-pressure conditions over temperatures ranging from room temperature to above melting.
Interatomic potentials derived from DFT encode short-range order and chemical-interaction effects in HEAs.
Short-range order and chemical interactions encoded in DFT-derived interatomic potentials mediate the solid-to-liquid transition in HEAs.
DFT provides a first-principles description of bonding and electronic-structure contributions to melting and fusion.
Machine-learning aggregation captures nonlinear composition effects and the complex interplay among alloying elements.
Capturing nonlinear composition effects enables efficient prediction of macroscopic fusion parameters without exhaustive experimental measurements.
The workflow will achieve errors no greater than 5% for the specified melting and liquid-state properties across a broad range of HEA compositions.
Traditional isolated experimental calibrations or empirical rules typically produce prediction errors exceeding 10% for HEAs.
The approach is expected to apply to HEAs that form well-mixed, single-phase solid solutions.
Strong electronic correlations, significant phase segregation, or kinetically dominated melting behavior may reduce the applicability of the workflow.
There is no direct evidence confirming that integrated DFT and machine learning consistently achieve errors within 5% across all HEA compositions.
Chemical complexity and unforeseen interactions may prevent consistent predictive accuracy across HEAs.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction errors exceed 5% in more than 30% of the tested HEA compositions.
